title: Wasserman’s Inc. v. Township of Middletown
summary: A lease-cancellation payment based on gross receipts required factual examination of its reasonableness; the court preserved reimbursement for improvements but did not finally uphold or invalidate the receipts formula.
notes: The printed total has a one-cent variation between the narrative and arithmetic display. This summary uses approximate totals and retains the original pages. The court expressly reserved consumer-contract enforcement rather than generalizing its commercial presumption to all parties.

sections.Parties: Wasserman’s was the original commercial tenant of township property. Jo-Ro operated the store as subtenant and shared rights to a cancellation payment. Middletown was the municipal lessor that cancelled and sold the property.
sections.Material Facts:
The thirty-year lease provided a relatively low fixed monthly rent and permitted cancellation upon payment of two components: a prorated amount for improvements and twenty-five percent of average annual gross receipts, calculated from the preceding three fiscal years. Wasserman’s improved and enlarged the store, then sublet it to Jo-Ro. The township cancelled with almost twelve years remaining and later sold the property for $610,000.

The gross-receipts calculation produced approximately $290,310. Jo-Ro’s tax returns, by contrast, reported modest profits of $3,649 and $414 and then a $323 loss in the relevant years. Those figures raised a concern about overcompensation but did not conclusively establish the actual loss: tax accounting, a valuable below-market lease, relocation, and other consequences could affect the proper assessment.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court enforced the lease and cancellation clause on summary judgment, awarding approximately $346,058 plus interest, including $55,748 for improvements. The Appellate Division affirmed. The New Jersey Supreme Court affirmed the lease’s enforceability and the improvement award, but remanded the gross-receipts component for further findings in 1994.
sections.Issue: Was the stipulated receipts-based cancellation payment a reasonable compensatory remedy, or an unenforceable penalty?
sections.Holding: The existing record was insufficient to decide that question. The clause had to be assessed for reasonableness, with the township bearing the burden of demonstrating that the commercial stipulated-damages provision was unreasonable.
sections.Reasoning:
The court treated reasonableness under the circumstances as the central test. Difficulty estimating injury is relevant to that assessment rather than necessarily an independent prerequisite. A reasonable stipulated remedy can allocate risk, save litigation expense, and protect otherwise difficult-to-prove interests. Judicial scrutiny nevertheless prevents a compensatory provision from becoming punishment.

Gross receipts are an imperfect proxy because they omit operating expenses and may have little relationship to net loss. The very low reported profits therefore warranted attention. But the court did not declare all receipts formulas invalid or equate tax profit mechanically with economic loss. It directed consideration of commercial reasonableness, the circumstances of the cancellation, the selected measurement year, mitigation, and replacement-space costs. Whether the clause was enforceable was a legal question that could depend on those underlying findings.

The opinion discusses assessment at formation or breach and the significance of actual loss. That discussion should be kept distinct from jurisdictions that insist on a formation-only approach.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Wasserman’s shows why concern about a formula does not always justify deciding its validity on summary judgment. The lease’s economic value and the nature of the loss matter alongside sales figures.

topics.remedies: Separates the upheld improvement reimbursement from the remanded stipulated-payment issue.
topics.liquidated-damages: Makes reasonableness and the relationship to actual or anticipated harm central.
topics.risk-allocation: Recognizes the value of advance commercial planning while policing overcompensation.

mnemonic.rationale: A liquidated-damages clause on a lease
